concept.name: Three inside up
concept.definition: A three-candlestick bullish reversal pattern introduced by Gregory Morris as a confirmed bullish harami: a long black body in a downtrend is followed by a small white body contained within it (the harami), and then a third candle closing above the second candle's close. The third candle's higher close is the confirmation that distinguishes it from the unconfirmed two-candle harami.
concept.intuition: First the trend's selling stalls inside the prior big candle, then the next candle actually closes higher, confirming that buyers, not sellers, won the standoff.
concept.mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long black body; candle 2 is a white (non-doji) body engulfed by body 1; candle 3 closes above candle 2's close (many implementations require a white body). Shadow lengths are disregarded. Practitioners often seek further confirmation via a break of nearby resistance or a trendline.
concept.formula: Three inside up when C1 < O1 (long body), O1 > O2, C2 > C1, min(O2, C2) > C1, max(O2, C2) < O1, and C3 > C2.
concept.failure_modes: Backtested occurrence statistics show only moderate efficiency; many instances fail in strong downtrends despite the built-in confirmation. Signals forming far from support or on low volume underperform.
concept.misconceptions: It is not just 'any three rising candles'; the first two must form a genuine bullish harami with body containment. It is also a Morris-era formalization, not one of the classical Japanese patterns.
concept.example: After a decline, a stock prints a long black candle (50.00 to 47.00), a small white candle inside it (47.50 to 48.30), then a third candle closing at 48.90, above the second close. The three inside up confirms the harami as a bullish reversal signal.
